title: Management of cocaine-associated chest pain and myocardial infarction: A scientific statement from the American Heart Association Acute Cardiac Care Committee of the Council on Clinical Cardiology

claims.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether a beta-blocker given in hospital to people with chest pain after cocaine use makes the narrowing of the heart's arteries, heart attacks or deaths more likely. That cocaine itself narrows the coronary arteries and reduces blood flow to the heart muscle for a time was shown in a randomized, double-blind laboratory study of 30 patients undergoing cardiac catheterization for chest pain, none of whom had used cocaine before (Dallas, published 1990): 15 minutes after intranasal cocaine 2 mg/kg (110 to 210 mg, a study condition the authors chose as one half to two thirds of the amount used for local anaesthesia of the nose and throat), against intranasal saline, systolic blood pressure rose by 11 mm Hg (95% CI 5 to 16), coronary sinus blood flow fell by 17 mL/min (5 to 29) and coronary vascular resistance rose, and six measured artery segments narrowed by 0.10 to 0.25 mm (about 6% to 10%, editors' calculation), significantly in four; no one had chest pain or electrocardiographic signs of ischaemia after cocaine alone (Lange et al., 1990). In a second study by the same group, the same dose reduced the area of disease-free artery segments by about 9% and 17% in its two arms (editors' calculation from the means; Boehrer et al., 1993). In the 1990 study, 10 of the patients given cocaine then received the beta-blocker propranolol infused directly into the left coronary artery (2 mg over 5 minutes): coronary sinus flow fell further, from 120 to 100 mL/min (change from the post-cocaine value −20 mL/min, 95% CI −42 to −1, P = 0.050), and resistance rose further (+0.16 mm Hg/mL per min, −0.02 to 0.33, P = 0.074), although the abstract reports P < 0.05 for both; nothing changed further in 5 patients given an intracoronary saline infusion after cocaine, nothing changed in 5 given propranolol after intranasal saline, and the randomized comparison between the two groups given cocaine was not tested. In 5 of the 10 an artery segment narrowed by more than 10%, and in one a coronary artery closed completely, with ischaemic symptoms and ST-segment elevation, which resolved after sublingual nitroglycerin without a rise in creatine kinase. In the 1993 study, intravenous labetalol (0.25 mg/kg), which blocks alpha as well as beta receptors, given to 9 such patients after cocaine lowered mean arterial pressure from 117 to 110 mm Hg but left the narrowed artery area unchanged (3.47 to 3.37 mm²); heart rate did not change at any point, so beta-blockade was not shown, allocation to labetalol or to saline (6 patients) was not described as randomized, and the two groups differed at baseline. Resting on these two studies (30 and 15 patients enrolled, of whom 10 and 9 received the blocker after cocaine; editors' count), on case reports and on animal experiments in which beta-blockers reduced coronary blood flow and increased seizures and deaths, the 2008 American Heart Association statement recommends that beta-blockers be avoided in the acute setting (Class III, Level of Evidence C, which it defines as consensus opinion of experts, case studies or standard of care), noting that no randomized trial of treatment for cocaine-associated infarction exists and that deaths from cocaine-associated infarction are very low, which alters the balance of risk and benefit; at discharge it reserves long-term beta-blockers for people with a documented infarction, a weakened left ventricle or ventricular arrhythmias, after counselling about cocaine use (McCord et al., 2008). In practice, 164 of 376 patients (44%) admitted with chest pain and a cocaine-positive urine screen at two St Louis hospitals in 2000–2007 were given a beta-blocker within 24 hours (metoprolol 74, labetalol 44, carvedilol 43, atenolol 3, so 87 received a drug that also blocks alpha receptors); they were older, had more hypertension and coronary disease, and received more aspirin, nitrates and other cardiac drugs, which were not adjusted for. In-hospital myocardial infarction, stroke, ventricular arrhythmia or death occurred in 16% of them and 12% of the others (odds ratio adjusted for propensity-score quintile 1.37, 95% CI 0.64 to 2.93); myocardial infarction in 5% against 2% (1.67, 0.44 to 6.35) and death in 3% against 6% (0.66, 0.14 to 3.04); the odds ratio was 1.83 (0.79 to 4.24) for beta-1-selective drugs and 0.90 (0.33 to 2.42) for carvedilol or labetalol, not tested against each other (Fanari et al., 2014). A meta-analysis of five retrospective US cohorts (1756 patients; 1794 in its abstract), pooling unadjusted counts, found no significant difference: non-fatal myocardial infarction in 94 of 610 patients (15.4%) given a beta-blocker and 162 of 1146 (14.1%) not given one (odds ratio 1.36, 0.68 to 2.74; I² 71%, single cohorts ranging from 0.18, 0.04 to 0.79, to 3.14, 1.42 to 6.95), and death in 6 of 348 (1.7%) against 22 of 666 (3.3%) (0.68, 0.26 to 1.79; three cohorts). It entered Fanari et al.'s percentages as event counts (5 and 2 for infarction, 3 and 6 for death); with the counts those percentages imply (about 8 of 164 and 4 of 212; 5 of 164 and 13 of 212) the pooled odds ratios are about 1.38 (0.70 to 2.69) for infarction and 0.56 (0.24 to 1.28) for death, still not significant (editors' calculation, which reproduces the printed results exactly from the printed counts). Its text attributes the one significant increase in infarction to the cohort that found a significant decrease, and it describes the two laboratory studies as giving 45 people intravenous beta-blockers (Pham et al., 2018). The laboratory studies measured artery size and blood flow for minutes after one moderate dose in people who had never used cocaine, with propranolol infused into a coronary artery rather than given by vein or by mouth; the hospital cohorts could not tell whether cocaine was still active when the drug was given (urine screens stay positive for 2 to 3 days), gave the drug to sicker patients, mixed drugs with and without alpha-blocking action, and had too few events to exclude either harm or benefit. No randomized trial has compared beta-blockers with other treatments in people with chest pain after cocaine.
claims.magnitude: Not estimable as an effect of beta-blockers on clinical outcomes. Laboratory, cocaine against saline (n = 15 each): coronary sinus flow −17 mL/min (95% CI −29 to −5), resistance +0.18 mm Hg/mL per min (0.13 to 0.24), artery segments −0.10 to −0.25 mm (about 6% to 10%, editors' calculation; 4 of 6 segments significant). Intracoronary propranolol after cocaine (n = 10), change from the post-cocaine value: flow −20 mL/min (−42 to −1; P = 0.050), resistance +0.16 (−0.02 to 0.33; P = 0.074); complete occlusion in 1 of 10. Intravenous labetalol after cocaine (n = 9): mean arterial pressure 117 to 110 mm Hg; artery area 3.47 to 3.37 mm² (unchanged). Hospital cohort (376 patients): composite in-hospital outcome 16% against 12%, adjusted odds ratio 1.37 (0.64 to 2.93); infarction 5% against 2%, 1.67 (0.44 to 6.35); death 3% against 6%, 0.66 (0.14 to 3.04). Meta-analysis of 5 cohorts (1756 patients): non-fatal infarction 15.4% against 14.1%, odds ratio 1.36 (0.68 to 2.74), I² 71%, single cohorts 0.18 to 3.30; death 1.7% against 3.3%, 0.68 (0.26 to 1.79), I² 0%; with Fanari et al.'s counts as their percentages imply (editors' calculation), 1.38 (0.70 to 2.69) and 0.56 (0.24 to 1.28).

claims.statement: In adults who came to a hospital emergency department with chest pain after recent cocaine use, a heart attack (acute myocardial infarction) was diagnosed in a small minority, from under 1 to about 6 in 100 depending on the study. At one urban US hospital (Flint, Michigan, July 1996 to February 1998) whose policy was to admit every such patient for at least 23 hours, with cardiac enzymes on arrival and every 8 hours for 24 hours, 15 of 250 admitted adults (6%) met World Health Organization criteria for infarction on serial CK-MB testing; the 95% confidence interval is printed as 3.1% to 8.9% in the Results and as 4.1% to 8.9% in the abstract, and the exact interval is 3.4% to 9.7% (editors' calculation) (Weber et al., 2000). Patients entered if they reported cocaine use in the previous week or had a positive urine screen (185 of the 196 tested were positive); they were young (mean age 33.5 years), mostly men (77%), African American (84%) and smoked tobacco (77%), and most had used cocaine within the previous 24 hours, mostly by smoking crack. They were found through hospital records coded for cocaine or other drug use, urine testing was routine only for patients aged 50 or under without cardiac risk factors, records coded for infarction were searched more thoroughly than others, and 9 patients sent home from the emergency department were left out, all of which would tend to raise the share; the authors also cannot exclude that a few small infarctions were missed. In hospital there were 7 complications (sustained ventricular tachycardia in 2 patients, supraventricular tachycardia in 3, heart failure in 1 and a slow heart rhythm in 1), none more than 12 hours after arrival, and all 250 patients left hospital alive; no complication after 12 hours in 250 patients is compatible with a true rate of up to 1.5% (editors' calculation). The 2008 scientific statement of the American Heart Association (a consensus document without a systematic search; these figures are second-hand) reports infarction in 6% of 246 patients in the prospective multicentre COCHPA study and in the Weber series, in 2.8% of 218 patients in another series (which Weber et al. describe as 2.5% of 241), and in 0.7% of 293 patients in the prospective ACI-TIPI study, which enrolled people with a wider range of symptoms at urban, suburban and semirural hospitals, and it attributes part of the spread to who was enrolled and to diagnostic criteria; Weber et al. add, also second-hand, that retrospective series ranged from 0% to 31% depending on whom they enrolled. The statement also reports, second-hand, that in COCHPA an electrocardiogram showing ischaemia or infarction detected only 36% of infarctions (specificity 89.9%); that in a randomized observation-unit study of 344 patients, 10 of the 42 high-risk patients admitted directly (24%) had an infarction, while among lower-risk patients observed for 9 to 12 hours there were no cardiovascular deaths and 4 of 256 followed up (1.6% to 2%) had a non-fatal infarction within 30 days; and that among 130 patients with cocaine-associated infarction in a 29-hospital US series, 38% had complications, 90% of them within 12 hours, and none died in hospital (McCord et al., 2008). In that 29-hospital series (1987–1993; 136 infarctions in 130 patients, found through hospital records), no one died in hospital among the 66 patients whose first electrocardiogram met the criteria then used for clot-dissolving (thrombolytic) treatment; of the 25 who were given it, by their clinicians' decision, none had bleeding into the brain or bleeding that needed transfusion and two had minor complications, but with 25 patients a rate of such major complications of up to about 14% cannot be excluded (exact 95% interval 0 to 13.7%, editors' calculation; printed 0 to 12%), and patients who were given the treatment but turned out not to have an infarction were not included; adding 11 earlier case reports, the authors count one fatal bleed into the brain in 36 treated patients (Hollander et al., 1995). These figures describe people who reached hospital in the 1980s and 1990s, mostly young men in US cities and mostly tested with CK-MB enzymes, the standard of the time; they are not the chance of a heart attack each time a person uses cocaine, and none of these studies compared patients with chest pain who had not used cocaine.
claims.magnitude: Infarction among adults admitted with chest pain after recent cocaine use at one hospital: 15 of 250 (6%; printed 95% CI 3.1–8.9%, abstract 4.1–8.9%; exact 3.4–9.7%, editors' calculation). Other emergency-department studies, second-hand: 6% of 246 (COCHPA), 2.8% of 218 (2.5% of 241 in Weber et al.'s description of the same study), 0.7% of 293 (ACI-TIPI); range 0.7% to 6%. Observation-unit study, second-hand: infarction in 10 of 42 high-risk patients admitted directly (24%) and non-fatal infarction within 30 days in 4 of 256 lower-risk patients. In-hospital course at the one hospital: 7 complications in 250 patients, none after 12 hours (upper 95% limit 1.5%, editors' calculation), no deaths. Confirmed infarction (29-hospital series): no in-hospital deaths among 66 ECG-eligible patients; no major complication in 25 given thrombolytic treatment (exact 95% CI 0–13.7%, editors' calculation); complications in 38% of 130, 90% within 12 hours, in-hospital mortality 0% (second-hand). ECG sensitivity for infarction 36%, specificity 89.9% (COCHPA, second-hand).
